lessons.bloodborne-pathogen-basics:
**Understanding Bloodborne Pathogens**

Bloodborne pathogens are disease-causing microorganisms that may be present in human blood. OSHA 1910.1030 specifically identifies hepatitis B virus (HBV) and human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) as important workplace hazards. Bloodborne pathogen exposure is not limited to hospitals or laboratories — in commercial and industrial settings, exposures can occur during first aid response, cleanup of contaminated surfaces, handling of contaminated sharps, contact with contaminated laundry or waste, or response to workplace injuries. OSHA 1910.1030 applies whenever employees have reasonably anticipated contact with blood or other potentially infectious materials (OPIM) as part of their job duties. Bloodborne pathogens are not always visible, and exposure can happen quickly — that is why established protective procedures must be followed every time.
lessons.exposure-control-plan:
**Occupational Exposure and the Exposure Control Plan**

The Exposure Control Plan is the employer's written program for eliminating or minimizing exposure to blood and OPIM. It must include an exposure determination (which job classifications and tasks have occupational exposure), procedures for implementing controls, and procedures for evaluating exposure incidents. The exposure determination must be made without considering PPE use. The plan must be accessible to all employees, reviewed and updated at least annually, and updated whenever new tasks or procedures are added. First aid responders, custodial employees, and certain maintenance staff are common examples of job classifications with occupational exposure. The Exposure Control Plan is not just a document — it is the roadmap for how the workplace identifies risks, selects controls, trains employees, and responds to incidents.
lessons.universal-precautions:
**Universal Precautions and Recognizing OPIM**

Universal Precautions is the practice of treating all human blood and certain body fluids as if they are known to be infectious, regardless of the apparent health status of the source person. OPIM includes body fluids visibly contaminated with blood and certain human tissues or fluids identified in the OSHA standard. When it is difficult or impossible to identify what type of body fluid is present, employees must treat it as potentially infectious. When providing first aid, always put on required PPE — gloves and eye protection at minimum — before making contact with blood or OPIM. If you are unsure about what you are dealing with, treat the material as infectious, keep others away, and follow your facility's cleanup and reporting procedures.
lessons.engineering-work-practice-controls:
**Engineering and Work Practice Controls**

Engineering controls isolate or remove the bloodborne pathogen hazard — examples include sharps containers, safer medical devices, and needleless systems. Work practice controls reduce exposure by changing how tasks are performed. Employees must wash hands immediately or as soon as feasible after removing gloves or other PPE and after any contact with blood or OPIM. Employees must never bend, break, or recap contaminated needles unless a specific one-handed technique or mechanical device is used. Contaminated broken glass must always be picked up using mechanical means such as tongs or a brush and dustpan — never bare hands or paper towels alone. Food, drink, tobacco, cosmetics, and contact lenses must be kept out of any area where exposure to blood or OPIM is possible.
lessons.personal-protective-equipment:
**Personal Protective Equipment**

PPE for bloodborne pathogen exposure may include gloves, gowns, lab coats, face shields, masks, eye protection, and resuscitation devices. PPE must be appropriate for the task and must prevent blood or OPIM from reaching skin, eyes, mouth, mucous membranes, clothing, or undergarments under normal use conditions. Employers must provide PPE at no cost to employees and ensure it is accessible in proper sizes. Disposable gloves must be replaced when they become contaminated, torn, punctured, or compromised — they must never be washed and reused. Contaminated garments must be removed as soon as feasible. PPE only works when it is the right equipment for the hazard, applied and removed correctly, and disposed of or decontaminated properly.
lessons.housekeeping-waste:
**Housekeeping, Spill Cleanup, Sharps, Waste, and Laundry**

Work areas must be maintained in a clean and sanitary condition. Contaminated surfaces must be decontaminated with an appropriate disinfectant after contact with blood or OPIM, after spills, and at the end of the work shift if contamination may have occurred. Contaminated sharps must be placed immediately in closable, puncture-resistant, leakproof, labeled or color-coded sharps containers — containers must be kept upright and replaced before they become overfilled. Regulated waste must be placed in closable, leakproof, labeled or color-coded bags or containers. Contaminated laundry must be handled as little as possible, with gloves, and placed in bags or containers at the location where it was used. When contaminated laundry may leak through, a secondary leakproof bag is required.
lessons.exposure-incidents-vaccination:
**Hepatitis B Vaccination and Exposure Incidents**

An exposure incident is specific eye, mouth, mucous membrane, non-intact skin, or parenteral contact with blood or OPIM that results from job duties. Employers must make the hepatitis B vaccine and vaccination series available to employees with occupational exposure at no cost, within 10 working days of initial assignment, unless the employee has previously received the series, antibody testing shows immunity, or the vaccine is contraindicated. After any exposure incident, employees must immediately wash exposed skin with soap and water, flush eyes or mucous membranes with water, report the incident, and follow the employer's post-exposure procedures. The employer must make a confidential medical evaluation and follow-up available immediately. Fast reporting is critical — it enables proper medical assessment, source testing when permitted, and timely treatment options.
lessons.labels-training-records:
**Labels, Signs, Training, and Records**

Warning labels using the biohazard symbol must be applied to regulated waste containers, refrigerators and freezers containing blood or OPIM, and other containers used to store, transport, or ship blood or OPIM. Red bags or red containers may be substituted for labels in certain situations under the standard. Bloodborne pathogen training must be provided at initial assignment and at least annually during working hours at no cost, in language and vocabulary employees can understand, with opportunity for questions and answers. Training records must include the training date, content summary or a copy of the training materials, the trainer's name and qualifications, and the names and job titles of all attendees. Training records must be maintained for three years from the training date.
